analysis.one_liner: Lets regulators fine insurers and middlemen who shortchange mental health coverage.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee hearing or a vote; it was introduced three weeks before the session ended and died in committee.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law since 2008 has required health plans to cover mental health and addiction care no more restrictively than medical care, but plans have faced little financial penalty for breaking that rule. This bill would let federal regulators impose civil monetary fines on plans and insurers that violate the parity requirement, and would extend liability to the companies that actually manage the benefits day to day — third-party administrators, managed behavioral health organizations, and pharmacy benefit managers — whenever they cause or contribute to a violation.
analysis.who_benefits: People with employer or individual health coverage who need mental health or substance use care. Today, when a plan quietly denies therapy visits, caps rehab stays, or charges high out-of-network rates for psychiatric care, there is little money at stake for the companies doing it. Attaching real fines — and making the administrators and PBMs who design those limits personally liable — gives regulators leverage to force plans to actually pay for the mental health care the law already promises.

how_it_helps.text: Allows the Secretary of Health and Human Services to collect civil monetary penalties from group health plans and insurers that fail to meet mental health parity requirements [S2].

Extends liability for parity violations to plan sponsors and service providers — including third-party administrators, managed behavioral health organizations, and pharmacy benefit managers — that cause or contribute to a violation, with the Secretary able to apportion the penalty among them [S2].
Gives states parallel authority to enforce parity requirements against plan sponsors and service providers, not just insurers [S2].
Applies these rules to plan years starting one year after enactment, so the penalties would attach quickly [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers, employee benefit administrators, managed behavioral health companies, and pharmacy benefit managers, which would face fines when their coverage rules treat mental health care worse than medical care. Some of those costs could be passed along in premiums or absorbed through tighter plan design; employers as plan sponsors could also share liability.

drawbacks.text: Penalties and liability exposure raise compliance costs for health plans and the companies that administer them, and some of that cost could show up in premiums paid by employers and workers [S2].

Holding third-party administrators and PBMs liable for plan design choices they make at an employer's direction spreads blame across parties in ways that could produce disputes over who ultimately owes a fine, which the bill leaves to the Secretary's discretion to apportion [S2].

Employers who sponsor self-insured plans would face new liability exposure for parity failures, which some would answer by narrowing or repricing benefits rather than expanding mental health access [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real: parity has been the law since 2008, yet mental health and addiction care is still routinely harder to get than other care, largely because violations carried little financial consequence. This bill attacks exactly that gap by adding fines and reaching the middlemen who operate the coverage. The costs are administrative and would fall partly on plans and employers, with some pass-through to premiums — a trade most supporters would consider worthwhile, though the liability apportionment could get messy in practice.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate health committee with three weeks left in the session, and no one acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Christopher Murphy introduced the bill in the Senate on December 12, 2024, with Sens. Smith and Luján as original cosponsors [S2].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on the day it was introduced [S4].
The bill's only cosponsors were two Democrats, and no Republican signed on [S3].
No committee hearing, markup, floor action, or vote followed; the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill's action history ends at the committee referral [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers, third-party administrators, managed behavioral health organizations, and pharmacy benefit managers are better off, because they continue to face no civil monetary penalties for parity violations — the bill died without any of its provisions taking effect. People who need mental health coverage remain in the same position as before.

for.name: Sen. Christopher Murphy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Parity Enforcement Act of 2024 in the Senate on December 12, 2024 [S2].

for.name: Sens. Tina Smith and Ben Ray Luján
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's only cosponsors at introduction [S3].

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired in the 118th Congress by Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-VT)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on December 12, 2024 and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or report — before the Congress ended [S4].

against.name: Health insurers and pharmacy benefit managers
against.role: Industries that would bear the penalties and liability
against.what_they_did: The industries with the most money at stake did not support the bill; strong parity enforcement has long been opposed by insurers and PBMs who profit from restrictive mental health benefit management.

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors and both cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the bill never advanced far enough for a recorded vote.

industries.note: The bill would expose insurers to civil monetary fines when their plans cover mental health and substance use care worse than medical care. Today those violations carry little financial penalty, so insurers benefit from the status quo that the bill would end.

PBMs design the drug-benefit side of parity — things like restrictive mental health drug tiers and prior authorization — and the bill would make them directly liable for parity violations they cause or contribute to.

industries.industry: Third-party administrators and managed behavioral health organizations
industries.note: These companies operate day-to-day benefit rules for employer plans and would face shared liability for parity failures, with the Secretary deciding how fines are split among plan, sponsor, and provider.
Plan sponsors would share liability for parity violations, a new cost and legal exposure; some might respond by tightening benefits rather than expanding mental health coverage.
